notes.bp: A spoken question-answering system needs training examples even when a language has little labeled data.
notes.wh: Synthetic text can be plentiful but may not resemble spoken questions; gains can come from artifacts or from better coverage, and the two must be separated.
notes.naive: Generate arbitrary question-answer pairs or train only on the small human set and assume more text automatically transfers to speech.
notes.ap: Use large-language-model-generated question-answer data and test its value separately on text QA, spoken QA, and Turkish spoken QA.
notes.mech: The study evaluates LLM-generated data for low-resource spoken QA across SQuAD, Spoken SQuAD, and Turkish spoken QA.
notes.math: Data generation is a controlled source of coverage: the useful question is not whether synthetic examples look plausible, but whether they improve the target speech task under restricted human supervision.
notes.ww: The paper reports relative F1 gains over restricted human-annotated training in the tested text and spoken QA settings.
notes.limits: Prompting, filtering, language, synthetic distribution, and evaluation splits limit transfer; synthetic gains do not establish factual or linguistic quality everywhere.
notes.title: Evaluating Large Language Models in Data Generation for Low-Resource Scenarios: A Case Study on Question Answering

notes.bp: We want to infer how the entire vocal tract moves from sound, including hidden parts such as the velum and glottis.
notes.wh: Acoustics are an indirect and many-to-one view of articulation; different configurations can produce similar sound, and real-time MRI labels are expensive.
notes.naive: Infer only easily sensed articulators or use a small sensor-based corpus and extrapolate to the full tract.
notes.ap: Train acoustic-to-articulatory models against complete vocal-tract contours from real-time MRI and compare individual and joint articulator prediction.
notes.mech: The paper reconstructs the complete vocal-tract contour from acoustic input using real-time MRI data and bidirectional recurrent models.
notes.math: The problem is inverse measurement: the model estimates hidden physical configuration from its acoustic consequence, so pixel-scale error and anatomical coverage matter as much as waveform fit.
notes.ww: The paper reports average contour RMSE near the MRI pixel size on its test set.
notes.limits: Speakers, MRI protocol, segmentation, speech styles, and model assumptions limit generalization; contour accuracy is not a complete articulatory theory.
notes.title: Reconstruction of the Complete Vocal Tract Contour Through Acoustic to Articulatory Inversion Using Real-Time MRI Data

notes.bp: Emotion recognition should continue working when a camera, transcript, or other modality is missing rather than failing because the training setup expected every input.
notes.wh: Modalities are correlated but not interchangeable; reconstruction can fill a missing channel while also inventing information that was never observed.
notes.naive: Train separate models for every modality combination or drop examples with missing inputs.
notes.ap: Align modalities contrastively and use masked reconstruction in one modality-agnostic model, then test unimodal, multimodal, and missing-modality cases.
notes.mech: The paper proposes a contrastive masked-autoencoder model for modality-agnostic multimodal emotion recognition on MSP-Podcast.
notes.math: The model learns shared structure while treating missingness as a normal observation condition; reconstruction supplies a bridge, but prediction must still be judged against the available evidence.
notes.ww: The paper reports improvements over unimodal and multimodal baselines and robustness to missing modalities.
notes.limits: Corpus, emotion labels, missingness pattern, modality quality, and reconstruction objective bound the claim; emotion inference is not guaranteed to be socially reliable.
notes.title: Modality-Agnostic Multimodal Emotion Recognition using a Contrastive Masked Autoencoder

notes.bp: A singing voice converter should transfer vibrato deliberately because vibrato carries style and emotion, but it must preserve the singer's identity and the song's content.
notes.wh: Vibrato is a fast variation within the fundamental-frequency contour, so treating it as undifferentiated pitch can make it hard to extract or control.
notes.naive: Leave vibrato entangled in the pitch representation or control it with a single average F0 value.
notes.ap: Separate high-frequency F0 variation with a wavelet transform, then explicitly transfer and control the vibrato component during conversion.
notes.mech: VibE-SVC extracts vibrato from the high-frequency F0 contour for controllable singing voice conversion.
notes.math: Style becomes an editable signal component: the system changes a time-varying pitch pattern while preserving the slower melody and speaker identity.
notes.ww: The paper reports objective and subjective evidence for high-quality conversion, style control, and speaker similarity.
notes.limits: Singers, songs, vibrato ranges, extraction errors, and evaluation conditions limit generalization; explicit control does not guarantee a preferred artistic result.
notes.title: VibE-SVC: Vibrato Extraction with High-frequency F0 Contour for Singing Voice Conversion

notes.bp: Language identification must work on very short speech, where two seconds may contain fillers, overlap, names, or even no speech.
notes.wh: A separate teacher model is expensive, and ordinary hard labels do not express uncertainty among languages or the fact that a segment may be out of scope.
notes.naive: Train on hard language labels only or distill from a large teacher and ignore the particular errors caused by short segments.
notes.ap: Use online soft labels from correctly classified training segments, with dynamic weighting, conditional updates, and entropy-based uncertainty, without a separate teacher.
notes.mech: The paper proposes teacher-free knowledge distillation for short-utterance spoken language identification.
notes.math: The soft target is an accumulated view of what the model reliably knows; uncertainty and segment quality shape how much each example changes the decision boundary.
notes.ww: The paper reports consistent Cavg improvements in same-corpus and cross-corpus short-utterance evaluations.
notes.limits: Languages, out-of-scope composition, duration, label updates, and corpora bound the result; better short-segment ID does not solve open-set detection generally.
notes.title: Teacher-Free Knowledge Distillation for Improving Short-Utterance Spoken Language Identification

notes.bp: A compact audio language model should detect spoofed speech without turning every unfamiliar recording into a spoof, even after quantization for deployment.
notes.wh: Zero-shot models can have strong-looking accuracy while carrying a severe class bias; quantization changes internal precision but may not be the main failure.
notes.naive: Report aggregate accuracy on clean data and assume FP16 or INT8 preserves the task behavior.
notes.ap: Evaluate several audio language models across spoof datasets and precisions, inspecting class bias and practical discrimination rather than accuracy alone.
notes.mech: The paper tests quantized audio language models for zero-shot spoofing detection on ASVspoof2019, In-the-Wild, and WaveFake.
notes.math: Deployment compression and task validity are separate questions: a model may retain its behavior after quantization while that behavior is already a biased near-random decision rule.
notes.ww: The paper reports negligible FP16 degradation but severe spoof-prediction bias that undermines practical detection.
notes.limits: Models, datasets, thresholds, quantization methods, and zero-shot prompts bound the claim; tested robustness is not security certification.
notes.title: Can Quantized Audio Language Models Perform Zero-Shot Spoofing Detection?

notes.bp: Speaker embeddings for conversational telephone speech need to work across speakers and languages under a fixed or open training-data rule.
notes.wh: Frontend architecture, pooling, pretraining, and training data all change the speaker geometry; a benchmark comparison can hide which component caused an improvement.
notes.naive: Choose one embedding architecture or use a large pretrained model without separating data condition, pooling, and domain effects.
notes.ap: Analyze several frontend families and pooling choices under the NIST SRE24 fixed and open conditions, including multilingual training data.
notes.mech: The paper analyzes ABC frontend audio systems for the NIST SRE24 audio track.
notes.math: The frontend is a measurement pipeline: representation, temporal pooling, training population, and domain match jointly determine whether identity survives telephone speech.
notes.ww: The paper reports comparative robustness and performance for the explored architectures and data conditions.
notes.limits: NIST protocol, telephone channel, language mix, training-data access, and calibration limit claims beyond the benchmark.
notes.title: Analysis of ABC Frontend Audio Systems for the NIST-SRE24

notes.bp: A medical summarizer may invent a fact about a patient-clinician conversation, so a detector needs controlled examples as well as naturally occurring failures.
notes.wh: Hallucinations are rare and variable; general-domain detectors may confuse missing evidence with a false claim, especially when the source is speech-derived clinical dialogue.
notes.naive: Evaluate only on generic hallucination data or label summaries without controlling which source fact was removed.
notes.ap: Construct a fact-controlled leave-one-out dataset and a natural hallucination dataset, then compare detection methods in the clinical setting.
notes.mech: The paper studies fact-controlled diagnosis of hallucinations in medical text summarization from patient-clinician dialogues.
notes.math: A controlled deletion makes the missing fact known, while natural cases test ecological validity; the two together separate detector sensitivity from dataset artifacts.
notes.ww: The paper reports that general-domain detectors struggle on clinical hallucinations and evaluates specialized diagnostic approaches.
notes.limits: Synthetic deletion, clinical language, annotation, summarizer, and detector thresholds limit generalization; detection is not prevention or clinical validation.
notes.title: Fact-Controlled Diagnosis of Hallucinations in Medical Text Summarization
